sections.title: Taxonomy and form
sections.text: Phaeocollybia christinae (Fr.) R. Heim, Christina’s rootshank, is a small agaric with a rust-brown spore print. Older sources place it in Hymenogastraceae or Cortinariaceae; a 2026 phylogenomic study recognizes Phaeocollybiaceae for the genus within Agaricales. Its most striking feature is the stem continuing underground as a long, tapering, often dark pseudorhiza.

sections.title: Cap, gills and stem
sections.text: The cap is usually a few centimetres across, pointed-conical at first and then conico-convex, with a sharp umbo. It is smooth and often viscid in wet weather, orange-red to reddish brown; as it dries, it fades toward ochre or tawny. The gills are crowded and narrowly attached to the stem, yellow-orange at first and later rust to reddish brown. The above-ground stem is slender, firm and smooth, yellow-orange near the gills, reddish in the middle and dark red-brown where buried. The flesh is sparse and fibrous-cartilaginous; a faint radish-like odour is sometimes reported.

sections.title: Pseudorhiza and ecology
sections.text: The long pseudorhiza is the stem continuing into the soil, not a plant root; its full tip can be difficult to excavate without breaking it. European collections are reported from conifer woods and also from beech (Fagus) and oak (Quercus) stands. These are collection habitats and do not by themselves prove a host relationship. The trophic role of Phaeocollybia remains under discussion: a study of the genus examines several hypotheses and reports evidence in favour of a mycorrhizal association, while regional sources do not all describe the same way of life.

sections.title: Food status and identification
sections.text: A regional mycological society describes it as inedible; do not collect it for food. Cap, gills and pseudorhiza may not by themselves confirm the species: Phaeocollybia species can be similar, and identification may require microscopic examination of the spores. This entry describes the taxon and cannot securely identify a found specimen.

traits: Small pointed-conical cap with a sharp umbo, orange-red to reddish brown, often viscid when wet and more ochre when dry
Crowded, narrowly attached gills, yellow-orange then rust to reddish brown
Slender, smooth, firm above-ground stem, yellow-orange near the cap, reddish in the middle and dark below ground
Stem extends underground as a long, tapering pseudorhiza, whose tip is often difficult to excavate intact
Reported in conifer woods and in beech or oak stands; trophic ecology remains debated
Rust-brown spore print; described as inedible in regional mycological sources
safetyNote: Phaeocollybia christinae is described as inedible. Do not use this page to identify or eat a wild mushroom; identification within the genus may require microscopic analysis.
